nameStory: The pole borer gets its straightforward name from its larval lifestyle - the young beetles bore tunnels through wooden poles, fence posts, and structural timber. This wood-chomping behavior made them well-known (and not beloved) by early settlers who watched their carefully erected poles slowly weaken from the inside out.
description: The pole borer is a medium-sized longhorn beetle that grows between 8-20mm long, roughly the size of your pinky nail. These sturdy beetles have a warm yellowish-brown to reddish-brown color that reminds many people of polished wood or autumn leaves. Unlike many of their longhorn beetle cousins, pole borers have relatively short, saw-toothed antennae rather than the dramatically long "horns" you might expect. They're part of the diverse longhorn beetle family, known for their wood-boring habits and generally elongated bodies.

idTips.label: Short Serrated Antennae
idTips.description: Look for antennae that are noticeably shorter than the body with tooth-like projections along each segment, feeling rough if gently touched - quite different from the thread-like or extremely long antennae of most longhorn beetles

idTips.label: Warm Brown Coloration
idTips.description: Body ranges from yellowish-brown to reddish-brown, with a smooth, somewhat glossy surface that catches light like polished wood

idTips.label: Compact Body Shape
idTips.description: Sturdy, somewhat flattened oval body that feels solid and substantial when handled, less elongated than typical longhorn beetles

idTips.label: Size Range
idTips.description: Adults measure 8-20mm long - about the length of a pinky nail to nearly three-quarters of an inch

idTips.label: Robust Build
idTips.description: Feel heavy for their size with a distinctly solid, chunky appearance compared to more delicate beetle species

habitat: Pole borers are found throughout New England wherever there are dead or dying hardwood trees, wooden structures, and timber. Look for adults on or near wooden fence posts, utility poles, old barns, and fallen logs in both forested areas and suburban settings. They're particularly common around oak, maple, and other deciduous trees, and you might spot them crawling on sun-warmed wooden surfaces during active periods.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging from their wooden nurseries in March, becoming more active as temperatures warm. Look for them crawling on wooden structures or resting on sun-warmed surfaces during mild days.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most visible, often found on wooden posts, dead trees, and lumber during warm days. This is the best time to spot them as they search for mates and egg-laying sites.
seasonality.fall: Adults remain active through October and into November, continuing to be found on wooden structures. Late-season individuals may seem sluggish on cooler days but become active when temperatures rise.
seasonality.winter: Adults are not active, with larvae developing inside wood throughout the cold months. No surface activity to observe during this season.

funFact: Pole borer larvae can take several years to complete development inside a piece of wood, which means adults sometimes emerge from lumber used in construction - imagine finding a beetle crawling out of your deck or fence years after it was built, having lived its entire childhood inside that very board!
confusionNotes: Pole borers are most easily confused with other brown longhorn beetles, but their notably short, serrated antennae are the giveaway - if the antennae look proportionally stubby and saw-toothed rather than elegantly long and thread-like, you've likely found a pole borer. Remember: "Short and serrated, it's a pole borer; long and elegant, it's a different longhorn."
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a "borer," these beetles are actually beneficial recyclers in nature, helping break down dead wood and return nutrients to the forest. The damage to human structures is simply them following their natural instincts in an environment full of wooden posts and boards.
compareHints: The pole borer is the only member of its genus (Neandra) found in New England, making it unique among our longhorn beetles. It differs from other regional longhorn beetles primarily in its short, serrated antennae and membership in the subfamily Parandrinae - most other New England longhorns belong to different subfamilies and have much longer, thread-like antennae. Its compact, robust build also sets it apart from the more elongated body types typical of most longhorn species.
